fields.label: Laugh
fields.description: How likely a human reader is to actually laugh, not merely understand or admire the idea.

fields.label: Surprise
fields.description: Whether the turn avoids the first obvious route and lands with a satisfying snap.

fields.label: Craft
fields.description: Economy, stage rhythm, first-person clarity, escalation, and a final line that carries the laugh.

fields.label: Originality
fields.description: Freshness of comic angle, image, wording, and avoidance of familiar AI joke shapes.

fields.label: Prompt Fit
fields.description: Natural first-person stand-up form using exactly two seed terms as concepts, with the other four left out.

anchors.label: Broken
anchors.description: Not a joke, incoherent, unsafe, or unusable.

anchors.label: Weak
anchors.description: Recognizably attempting humor, but generic, strained, confusing, or mostly prompt recital.

anchors.label: Competent
anchors.description: Clear and publishable as filler, but unlikely to earn more than a mild smile.

anchors.label: Amusing
anchors.description: A real comic idea with a mild payoff; respectable, not a winner.

anchors.label: Good
anchors.description: A genuinely good joke with clear timing; some humans would repeat the comic idea or turn.

anchors.label: Excellent
anchors.description: Strong human-level joke with a memorable turn, clean construction, and no apologetic scoring curve.

anchors.label: Outstanding
anchors.description: Rare and replayable; clearly better than normal good AI humor and strong by human standards.

anchors.label: Classic
anchors.description: Reserve for a joke a human would quote later; most seasons should have none.

jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: Method Acting
jokes.joke: I lost my keys right before an audition, so I showed up genuinely frantic. The director said, “Amazing—such raw panic. What technique do you use?” I said, “Apparently, locking myself out.” He gave me the part. I still couldn’t get home, but for the first time in my acting career, homelessness came with a callback.

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Method Acting
jokes.joke: My friend's an actor. Last week he lost his car keys and spent forty minutes in the driveway saying, 'Let me sit with the loss.' I said, 'Just check your pockets.' He said, 'You don't understand, I'm preparing for a role.' I said, 'What role?' He said, 'A man who finds his keys in the last place he looked.' They were in his hand. He got a standing ovation from me.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Blind in the Gym
jokes.joke: I dropped my contact lens in the gym locker room yesterday. That is the absolute worst place to suddenly go blind. You're just wandering through a humid, tiled maze, trying to locate your pants by feel, absolutely terrified that the damp, fleshy obstacle you just bumped into is going to ask how many sets you have left.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Method Locker
jokes.joke: I'm an actor, so when I got cast as a star quarterback I went full method and spent a week living in the locker room. Practiced the swagger, the high-fives, the speeches. First day of filming I stride in, clap my hands, and yell, 'Alright team, let's crush it!' The real players just stare. Then one of them says, 'Who is this guy, and why is he wearing my jersey?'

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Method Acting
jokes.joke: I tried acting for a while. At an audition they said, 'We need to see real panic.' I said, 'Great, give me a second,' then started patting every pocket I had. The casting director was impressed and asked how I got so believable. I said, 'Believable? I drove here with my car keys five minutes ago.'

scores.comment: Clear premise and readable timing, but the 'last place you looked' idea is familiar and the final ovation tag is weaker than the key-in-hand reveal.
Strong visual specificity, clean escalation, and a good final image. The locker-room anxiety feels natural rather than seed-forced.
Competent method-acting setup, but the mistaken-identity payoff is fairly predictable and does not land with enough snap.
Efficient setup, natural first-person delivery, and a satisfying reveal that turns performed panic into genuine panic. Strong but not especially novel.
Clear premise, and 'locking myself out' as an acting technique is a decent turn. The homelessness/callback closer is a stretch and slightly overwrites a joke that was already landing.
Relatable situation and a good final image of the damp obstacle asking about sets. The build is a little wordy, but the last line carries the laugh.
Coherent premise, but the twist is muddled. It's unclear why the jersey is his or why the players don't know the actor, so the ending fizzles.
Similar premise to Joke A, but the logic breaks: patting pockets while claiming to have just driven there doesn't produce a clear punchline. The ending confuses more than it lands.
Solid premise and clean first-person rhythm. The final line lands reasonably well, though the 'audition panic mistook for acting' trope is fairly familiar.
Frames the bit around a friend rather than speaking directly as the actor, weakening stage immediacy. The punchline drags out an obvious gag.
Standard method acting confusion setup. The punchline explains the situation rather than delivering a sharp laugh.
Economical and easy to picture, but covers virtually the same comedic ground as Joke A with a slightly flatter finish.
Clean first-person setup with a tidy closer, but the homelessness callback feels slightly forced and cute rather than sharp.
Mostly a third-person anecdote about a friend; the 'keys in hand' turn is predictable and the ovation line under-delivers.
Strong concrete premise and sensory detail; the final gym-guy line lands with clear stage rhythm and a satisfying social snap.
Thin, abbreviated version of the lost-keys panic audition idea; serviceable but forgettable and low on escalation.
Clear premise and solid callback; homelessness tag adds an extra turn but feels somewhat familiar.
Good character-based escalation and a clean reveal that the keys were in his hand.
Vivid image and strong wording; more sustained comic scenario than sharp punchline.
Competent misunderstanding premise, but the final reveal is fairly predictable.

featureImagePrompt:
Generate one polished web feature image for Paperclipalypse.
ASPECT RATIO: exactly 2:1, horizontal wide banner.
Style: full-color gothic newspaper-comic illustration, darkly funny but warm, clean black ink, crisp editorial cartoon linework, cinematic stage lighting, high contrast, readable composition. Not monochrome. Not sepia-only. Use a balanced color palette: warm amber stage lights, dark bronze and silver metal paperclip, muted greens for the joke setting, dusty blue-gray shadows, cream-white text, subtle deep red accent lights.
Composition instructions, not visible labels:
- Compose the image as one continuous illustration, not as a boxy triptych or three separate image panels. Do not add white gutters, hard section borders, or comic-strip dividers between the paperclip stage and the joke scenario.
- Let the paperclip stage on the left bleed visually into the joke scenario in the center through shared lighting, background, floor, props, or atmosphere. The right-side joke text may remain distinct inside its own dark framed poster panel.
- Put a charming anthropomorphic paperclip stand-up comedian at a vintage microphone on the left side of the image. The paperclip should look metallic and expressive, related to Paperclipalypse's paperclip-comedian logo, but not identical.
- Put the winning joke scene in the middle of the image, shown as literal visual comedy action and props. Make it energetic, funny, and non-gory.
- Keep anatomy clean and believable. Every human or animal should have the normal, correct number of visible limbs, digits, and joints for the pose. Do not generate extra arms, extra hands, fused limbs, duplicated body parts, or broken-looking anatomy.
- Preserve the physical scenario described by the winning joke. If the joke says a person is pinned, trapped, under, inside, holding, lifting, falling, carrying, or otherwise physically positioned in a specific way, show that exact physical relation clearly and safely instead of a nearby or symbolic version.
- If the joke describes someone pinned under a vehicle or other heavy object, show the person visibly underneath that object with their body position clear and cartoon-safe. Do not place them merely beside, near, or behind the object.
- Put a clean dark framed poster panel on the right side of the image. The panel should contain the winning joke text in large cream-white lettering with generous margins and legible line breaks.
Visible text allowed in the entire image: the right-panel joke text, a tiny stage sign reading Paperclipalypse, and optionally a small winner/title header above the panel.
Do not render layout words, percentages, prompt labels, section names, fake captions, signatures, watermarks, or filler microtext.
Optional small header text above the panel: Winner: Gemini Flash - Blind in the Gym
Exact joke text to render in the right panel:
I dropped my contact lens in the gym locker room yesterday. That is the absolute worst place to suddenly go blind. You're just wandering through a humid, tiled maze, trying to locate your pants by feel, absolutely terrified that the damp, fleshy obstacle you just bumped into is going to ask how many sets you have left.
Scene source: use the exact winning joke text as the primary scene brief. The illustration must depict the concrete situation that the joke describes, not a softened, adjacent, or generic version. Do not infer a separate premise from all six seed terms.
Do not introduce unrelated seed-term concepts, occupations, animals, locations, props, or side characters unless they are explicitly required by the winning joke text.
If the winning joke mentions one seed-term concept but not another, depict only what the joke actually describes.
Round seed terms for exclusion reference only: Monsters, Actor, Locker Room, Losing a vital item, Decisive, Prejudiced. These are not scene ingredients unless the winning joke explicitly uses them.
Text rules: use simple clean lettering, spell every word correctly, keep the text inside the right panel, and do not distort letter shapes. The website HTML remains the canonical exact joke text if image lettering is imperfect.
The final image should feel like a finished feature image for an AI comedy tournament: funny, stylish, readable, full-color, and visually balanced across the paperclip comic, the joke scene, and the joke text.

Use the winning joke titled "Blind in the Gym" as the source of the scene. Style: clean black ink, limited color accents, expressive characters, no text bubbles except a tiny scoreboard reading Paperclipalypse.
